Opposition parties shut down Indian parliament in solidarity with ‘cockroach’ protests Proceedings suspended as politicians call for Modi government to address police violence and education scandals India’s opposition parties have shut down parliament in a protest calling for the resignation of the education minister, in solidarity with the new youth-led “cockroach” movement. Opposition politicians, led by the Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi, gathered outside the parliament building in Delhi on Wednesday, many dressed in black and waving placards calling on Dharmendra Pradhan to quit. Inside the parliament chamber, proceedings were suspended after opposition figures demanded that Narendra Modi’s ruling government address the police violence against young people at a protest on Monday, and the scandals that have engulfed crucial exams. The previous day, Gandhi had been briefly detained by police after staging a sit-in outside Modi’s residence, accusing the prime minister of “destroying the future of India’s youth”. Gandhi’s sister, Priyanka, a senior Congress party strategist, was also briefly detained on Tuesday. Police confirmed they were later released. The opposition protests at parliament were in support of a new mass youth movement, known as the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), that began as a satirical online joke but has grown into a significant political challenge to the Modi government. On Monday, the CJP held one of the biggest anti-government protests in years. Dozens of people were injured after police used teargas and baton charges against the demonstrators. More than 1,000 people remained camped out at the CJP’s protest site in central Delhi on Wednesday despite the gruelling heat and humidity. Many of the protesters had travelled for miles to be there and vowed they would not move until the education minister had resigned and the Modi government listened to their demands. Food deliveries sent by supporters – some ordered from abroad – have continued to arrive, keeping the protesters well fed on biryani, pizza, rice and dal. Morale remained high as slogans and songs rang out across the site. “In the country where people had forgotten how to ask questions, in the country where criticising the government was considered treason – we have now awakened that country,” said CJP spokesman Ashutosh Ranka, to loud cheers from the crowd. The CJP’s demands for changes to the education system and the resignation of Pradhan arose after repeated scandals over testing, but it has grown into a larger movement giving voice to the frustration’s of India’s youth. It was estimated that more than 50,000 people had protested in Delhi on Monday, even though the police denied them permission to march on parliament. It began as a peaceful demonstration, but by late afternoon police began to clash with the protesters. Police said 60 civilians and 118 police personnel had been injured, and they accused protesters of instigating the clashes. But organisers condemned the “high-handedness” of the authorities and said hundreds of peaceful protesters had been injured by the police, including at least one woman now on a ventilator in intensive care from her injuries. Amnesty International have accused Delhi police of using police excessive force. India’s Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to hear a petition alleging police brutality against the protesters. Congress accused the Modi government of refusing to address the issues of the students and the alleged “brutality unleashed on students” in parliament. “The government doesn’t want to take any accountability, nor does it want to have a debate on it in parliament,” said Gandhi. Protests supporting the CJP movement were also held in Mumbai and Bengaluru, drawing hundreds of people. Modi has not commented directly on the protests, but the education minister, who had dismissed the CJP protesters as a “B-team of terrorists”, took a more conciliatory tone in his first comments since Monday’s protests. In a social media post, Pradhan said: “We owe them [students] answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering. He added: “The students of India deserve far better than being treated as props in a political campaign,” he said, referring to Gandhi’s protest. This article includes content provided by Instagram. Several key opposition parties have come out in support of the students’ movement and condemned the police violence against Monday’s protest. Sandeep Dikshit, a senior leader of the Congress party, said: “What happened yesterday is our constitution got trampled upon. After that, no self-respecting politician or citizen can stand aside.”

Police officer fatally shoots man in Madison, Wisconsin, sparking protests Shooting happened on street in popular neighborhood lined with restaurants, bars, shops and homes A police officer in Madison, Wisconsin, shot and killed a man on Wednesday in an incident that was captured on cellphone footage, sparking local protests. John Patterson, the Madison police chief, acknowledged the shooting at a news conference, but stressed footage circulating was just one perspective of what happened. “I want to take a moment to honestly and sincerely offer my heartfelt sympathies to his family for this loss,” Patterson said. The dead man was in his 30s, Patterson said, but police did not release his name. The shooting happened on a city street in a popular neighborhood lined with restaurants, bars, shops and residential homes less than 2 miles from the state capitol. Footage of the incident shows numerous cars stopped in the intersection with people watching as it unfolded. “Another Black man is dead on a Madison street, and our community watched him die before we even knew his name,” said Brandi Grayson, the head of Urban Triage, a Madison-based Black community advocacy group. “That is the cruelty of state violence.” A crowd formed near where the shooting occurred on Wednesday with people chanting: “Arrest the cops!” Police had been responding to calls that someone was attempting to enter parked vehicles in the neighborhood, Patterson said. The suspect fled on a bike through nearby backyards in an attempt to get away before officers contacted him in the street, Patterson said. The suspect either fell off his bike or was taken off his bike by officers and during the struggle pulled out a knife and injured an officer, Patterson said. In one of the videos circulating online, three officers are seen holding the man down and attempting to arrest him. The officers lose control of the suspect, who frees his arms and attempts to get up off his knees. One officer appears to reach for his pistol, when a female officer runs toward the others shouting: “Taser! Taser!” That officer did not draw his firearm. After some jostling, the suspect falls to the ground. As he goes down, another officer rises to his feet, pulls out his pistol, leans down toward the man on the ground and fires three shots at close range. The officer who fired the shots then re-holsters his gun and places the suspect’s arm behind his back, before standing up and walking away. Two other officers push the suspect over on to his belly, before others arrive to attempt to offer medical attention. The officer who fired the lethal shots had been injured by the suspect with a knife, Patterson said. He described the officer as a veteran of the police force, but didn’t provide his name. Another officer was injured, but it’s not clear how, Patterson said. The other two officers were uninjured. The race of the officer who fired his gun on Wednesday and that of the man killed were not released by police. But advocates for the Black community in Madison said the man killed was Black. Sabrina Madison, the city council president, called the videos “both disturbing and painful”, in a statement. “I’ve received several calls from alders with questions and what I can say without a doubt is that I expect a full, comprehensive, and transparent independent investigation into today’s shooting of a community member,” the statement reads. The Wisconsin department of justice criminal investigation will investigate the shooting because it involves police officers. A white police officer shot and killed Tony Robinson, who was biracial, on the same street in 2015, a shooting that spurred large protests. The district attorney did not file charges against police in that incident, determining the officer had been justified.

‘What if all cockroaches came together?’ The youth movement threatening to shake up India’s politics Cockroach Janta party began as online joke but is growing into one of the most unexpected challenges to country’s rightwing government The call out to the youth of India was simple: “Get ready to swarm the streets of Delhi with peaceful and loving dissent.” They came in their thousands. The weekend marked the first public protest of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a movement that began as an online joke, but which has swiftly grown into one of the most unexpected challenges to the indomitable power of the country’s rightwing Narendra Modi government – driven by millions of discontented and disillusioned young people. “The youth of this country will no longer fear, they will fight,” said CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, who had flown in that morning from the US to lead the lively protest. “For the government, we may be mere insects, but we are alive and capable of fighting for our rights.” Among the gen Zs and millennials who gathered amid a heavy police presence, many expressed hope that a youth-led mobilisation, similar to movements that brought down governments in the neighbouring countries of Nepal and Sri Lanka, could be gathering pace in India. “The young people here have suffered enough too,” said Kriti, 21, a university student from Delhi. The momentum behind the CJP has taken many by surprise, none more so than Dipke, who just a few weeks ago was living a quiet life in the US as an Indian graduate of Boston University. It was only on a whim, enraged by the comments of the chief justice of India who had compared India’s unemployed youth to “parasites” and “cockroaches” during a supreme court hearing, that Dipke had jokingly put out a call on social media: “What if all cockroaches came together?” The overwhelming response made him realise he had touched a nerve. He built a website and social media accounts for a satirical Cockroach Janta party – a poke at Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janta party (BJP) – complete with a biting manifesto taking aim at the government, and a tagline: “A political party for the people the system forgot to count.” Within two weeks, the CJP’s Instagram page had more than 22 million followers, far overtaking the BJP. Not long after, the Modi government, notoriously intolerant of dissent, had attempted to block its account on X on national security grounds. Though initially cloaked in satire, for many of India’s gen Zs and millennials, the CJP has given voice to their growing frustrations over an education system in crisis, and a job market that has been systematically failing them. According to one recent study, almost 40% of India’s graduates below 25 are unemployed. Questions still remain about whether the cockroach movement can transition from an online phenomenon to a genuine political mobilisation. To some, Saturday’s turnout of thousands was heartening, while others viewed it as a disappointment when compared to the tens of millions voicing support online. But out on the streets of Delhi few viewed the CJP as an AI internet meme any longer. “We are the future of this country and they have the audacity to call us cockroaches,” said Mehima Fatima, 26, a student at Delhi University. “It is so sad to see what has happened to education in this country. I hope this is the beginning of the resistance.” The rise of the CJP comes amid growing criticism of India’s “toxic” exam industry and its toll on the country’s youth. More is now spent in India on private tuition than the government’s entire higher education budget, with parents often getting into crippling debt to ensure their children get coveted places to study medicine and engineering or secure lucrative government jobs. The pressure on students to succeed has been linked to a growing number of suicides. Writing in his newspaper column this week, the analyst Pratap Bhanu Mehta said that “these examinations are not merely instruments of evaluation. They are instruments of social control, and extraordinarily effective ones at that … The message of the system is no longer to ask why or how, but simply to do and die.” Much of the “cockroach” movement has been mobilised around mounting student distress over exam chaos, after this year’s medical entrance exam – where more than 2 million students compete for just 130,000 places – was once again leaked to the highest bidder, forcing it to be scrapped and for students to face retaking the gruelling tests. A core demand of Saturday’s protest was the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, whom many hold responsible for the successive scandals. The leaks were widely seen as symptomatic of a “corrupt and broken” education system under the Modi government. “We are here to demand accountability,” said Ratna Singh, 30, who clutched a rose and a copy of the constitution, which protesters had been instructed to bring to the demonstration to show they came in peace. “People are slaving away for exams that get leaked, and at the end there are no jobs for us anyway. There is a need for a revamp of the entire education system.” Nonetheless, many of those who took to the streets to proudly declare themselves as “cockroaches” also acknowledged that the movement was a David and Goliath battle. Under Modi, the BJP has consolidated unprecedented amounts of power across government, media and the judiciary, and the state has routinely gone after political opponents and critics. Speaking to the crowds on Saturday, Dipke said he would be willing to sacrifice his freedom for the movement: “We have turned the joke into a revolution”.

India’s Cockroach movement protesters show no sign of backing down Thousands of people again on the streets of Delhi calling for education reforms despite police violence on Monday Taru had come to the protest prepared this time. In one hand was an anti-government poster and in the other was a bicycle helmet. “We need to have protection in case Delhi police beat us up again,” said the 25-year-old, who stood among her friends. “We are not scared of them and we won’t run away, no matter what they do. We’ll stay here till they listen.” On Tuesday, central Delhi still thronged with thousands of protesters, as an unprecedented expression of dissent against the powerful ruling Narendra Modi government showed no sign of abating. Just 24 hours earlier, more than 50,000 people took to the streets in protest, swathes of them in their late teens and early 20s, mobilised by a new youth-led political movement that calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP). Their rallying call was the resignation of the education minister and for reform of a corrupt and broken education system. But what began peacefully on Monday – people fanning each other in the gruelling humidity, sharing snacks and chanting slogans – turned into scenes of brutality by the afternoon. Delhi police denied the protesters the right to march on parliament and kettled the expanding crowd into a restricted area. The internet was shut down and barricades were erected across the capital. The came the police batons and the teargas. Police said they were responding to agitation but organisers and witnesses claimed the police carried out unprovoked attacks, including against women and children in the crowd. About 60 suffered injuries and at least one protester is on a ventilator in hospital intensive care. “The day was so wholesome to start with, there was so much love,” said Taru. “But after 3pm the police started attacking us. They were bashing us like anything. I saw them come up and hit people on the head as they were sitting down on the pavement doing nothing. And then as we were running, they opened up teargas on us.” Taru described the response by Delhi police – which are under central government control – as a “big mistake. Now we are more agitated than ever.” On Tuesday, the heavy hand of the Delhi police did little to keep supporters away from the historical site of Jantar Mantar in Delhi, which has become the focal point of the CJP protests over the past month. The crowds were thick and lively as they shouted slogans against the Modi government with abandon, calling for both the education minister and the prime minister to resign. Some had travelled hundreds of miles to be there and said they intended to camp out until the government responded to the demands of the country’s millions of young people. “The government needs to understand: we are not going anywhere,” said Ranjit Verma, 23. India’s main opposition Congress party had also seized upon the mood, calling for Modi to resign “for destroying the future of India’s youth” as it held its own protest in Delhi on Tuesday. While the CJP movement has primarily focused on accountability for devastating leaks of exam papers and calling for the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, the overriding feeling in the aftermath of Monday’s protest was that this was now so much bigger than one issue. For some, this was the moment India’s youth – totalling more than 600 million – had found its political voice. “The solidarity on the streets yesterday filled my heart,” said Kuhoo Kaushik, 26, a content creator from Delhi. “How the government responded was really sad, police beating up 14-year-olds is horrible. But personally, I feel like it’s really awoken something in me. “That’s why I’ve come back today: we won’t be moved until the government listens to us. It’s become about so much more than education – but one step at a time”’ Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke vowed that the protests would continue, though did not state what the next steps for the movement would be to capitalise on their momentum. Standing by the stage at the protest site, Ratna Singh, a CJP spokesperson, said the movement was very aware of ways in which the Modi government had successfully cracked down on previous movements and figures of dissent during its 12 years in power. “Anyone who has tried to speak up against this government has faced terrorism charges or tax raids or jail and there is so much fear,” she said. “But I am very proud at how many people have showed up and come out on the streets. The police showed us no mercy – but no matter what barbaric treatment they give us, we will not be silenced.” While a senior government minister met two CJP spokespeople on Monday to discuss their demands, Singh said the government had not responded to them on Tuesday and the “prime minister has remained silent about what happened”. It was not only young people who returned to the protest site on Tuesday. Shobha Varma, 80, was attending with her granddaughter. “Our education system has been failing young people for years,” she said. “But when I look out at everyone here, I really feel hope.”

Indian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spread Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall The Cockroach activist Sonam Wangchuk has ended a 26-day hunger strike, as youth-led protests continued to erupt across India and leaders of the movement said there was no breakthrough in talks with the government. Wangchuk had been fasting since June in solidarity with the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), a new youth-led movement that has been holding mass protests calling for government accountability and the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over exam paper leaks. The leaks affected 2 million students in May and have been linked to more than a dozen suicides. On Friday morning, Wangchuk posted that he had ended the hunger strike in Delhi after striking a “hard bargain” with the government. In a video from his hospital bed, he said he had been assured in writing that accountability in the examination system would be taken up on the parliament floor and that there would be no cases registered against young people who took part in mass protests in Delhi on Monday. After 26 days without food, Wanghuck appeared weak but in lively spirits. The hunger strike has long been a powerful tool of protest in India – repeatedly used by Mahatma Gandhi in the fight for Indian independence. Gandhi’s longest hunger strike was 21 days. After Wangchuk ended his hunger strike, Modi urged the activist to follow doctors’ advice and regain the weight he had lost. The CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, thanked Wangchuk for his “courage and sacrifice” and said the protests would continue until Pradhan resigned. “We won’t let Sonam ⁠sir’s sacrifice go in vain,” Dipke added. Protests erupted across India on Friday as part of the countrywide callout, with huge demonstrations in Bengalaru, Mumbai, Nagpur, Jaipur, Hyderabad, Chennai and Kolkata, some with turnouts of more than 100,000. On Friday, CJP leaders said the government had agreed to meet them in a “neutral location” to discuss their demands. However, in the aftermath of the meeting, the CJP’s spokesperson, Ashutosh Rank, said that no resolution had been agreed and the government had requested more time to consider their key demand, the resignation of Pradhan. “We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring ⁠this matter to a conclusion,” said Ranka. The senior government minister JP Nadda confirmed that talks between the two sides would resume on Saturday. As talks stalled on Friday, thousands of protesters continued to gather at CJP’s protest site in Delhi, in an unprecedented show of support for the dissenting movement. Tens of thousands more are expected to turn up over the weekend. Authorities shut down 17 metro rail stations near the protest site. In a move that was criticised by human rights groups, the government also ordered telecom companies to block mobile internet services in the area. However, it did little to stem the tide of people turning out. “It feels so positive out here,” said Afreen Ali, 21, a student at Delhi university, who stood among the crowds. “I’m feeling so mesmerised to see all my Indian brothers, my sisters, my youth, everyone out here protesting for their rights and for their education. It was the blood of our freedom fighters that brought us independence, and we are here to fight for that country.” The protests represent the biggest youth challenge to Modi since he came to power in 2014. ‌Opposition parties have echoed the youth movement’s demands and have ‌disrupted the monsoon session of parliament that began this week. On Thursday, Modi said special courts would be set up to prosecute those behind exam paper leaks, his first public response to the crisis. “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future ⁠of our youth!” he posted on social media. But the CJP rejected the proposal, saying what courts do after paper leaks is just one aspect of the problem. “But ​Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the ​first place?” said Ranka. “Fast-track ​courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues – you know the answer to that question, ​and so do we.” Later in the day, Modi ‌said on social media that the government ​would announce more strict actions against paper leaks at ​a cabinet meeting on Friday. After top Bollywood stars were hit with criticism for staying silent about the protests, some of India’s biggest actors, including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt and Kareena Kapoor, released social media posts saying it was heartening to see students come together to fight for a cause – though stopped short of criticising the Modi government.

India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked Even the night before Narendra Modi accepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government. Addressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who were mobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”. Less than 24 hours later, Modi, who has fiercely cultivated his strongman image for years, had bowed to public pressure and accepted the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. It was, say analysts, the remarkable humbling of a government that has ruled with almost untouchable impunity since 2014. Over that past week, a gen Z movement that called itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) mobilised unprecedented protests in the name of justice for millions of young people, after the leaking of a crucial exam paper forced 2 million students to resit the test and was blamed for more than a dozen suicides. The resignation of Pradhan, Modi’s loyal political ally, remained their first and foremost demand for accountability, even as the protests expanded into a wider fight for democracy. Yet Pradhan went unmentioned by Modi in his Instagram address. On Saturday morning, more people than ever were pouring into Delhi’s historic Jantar Mantar site – the centre of the protests – and unrest was spreading fast to other cities, including states ruled by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). It was not only physical space that had been captured by the cockroach movement. Since coming to power, the BJP has proved enormously effective at capturing the online narrative, deploying its powerful, highly organised IT cell to mobilise and attack any perceived criticism of the government, whether it came from citizens, politicians or journalists. But this proved no match for the millions of gen Z memes and reels that began to flood Instagram over this past week, fearlessly insulting Modi and pillorying the government, each more creative and incendiary than the next. Modi’s last-ditch attempts to speak directly to the youth on Instagram were simply met with more ridicule and spin-off memes. Modi had also lost another medium critical to the BJP’s domination over the national narrative – the mainstream TV news channels widely acknowledged to have been co-opted by the BJP government over the past 12 years and turned into mouthpieces for its rightwing Hindu nationalist ideology. Initially, the channels ignored the protests, and when they did cover them it was to suggest the protesters were being bankrolled by sinister foreign forces and Pakistani terror groups. In response, the protesters turned on the channels, using social media to expose their “lies”. When the protests escalated, Modi remained conspicuously absent from the airwaves. Pradhan’s resignation came as it appeared that all other options for the government had gone. The option of a ruthless crackdown appeared untenable given the mass outcry to the police violence that had hit protesters on Monday. “The online space was totally conquered by the protesters and regime-loving media was seriously delegitimised,” said Ashutosh Varshney, a professor of international studies at Brown University in Rhode Island. “The anger was so comprehensive there was no option left but for Pradhan to go.” But this was more than the loss of a minister, Varshney said, it was also the first time in 12 years that the Modi government had lost control of the political narrative. “This is a repressive government,” he said. “It wants obedience, it wants no critical discussion and it generates fear. But now the climate of fear has collapsed.” Analysts say the resignation of Pradhan could also have implications for Modi’s power over his own cabinet. Pradhan was one of Modi’s most loyal ministers and ideological footsoldiers, and had implemented policies exactly as senior party figures had wanted. He had also helped the BJP win Odisha state for the first time in the general election, bringing in crucial seats. “Modi knows once you start firing your most loyal ministers, it sets up the incentives for defections in other ministers as well,” said the political columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta. “If your own cabinet starts to hedge for a future where they may not be backed by your own government, that’s when you are in trouble.” Prior to this week’s unrest, Modi had been riding high on a string of important state electoral victories, in particular the BJP’s first triumph in West Bengal, a politically important state that had long pushed back against its Hindu nationalist politics. The BJP appeared to have fully bounced back from the blow in the 2024 elections, when the party failed to win an outright parliamentary majority and had to scramble together a large enough alliance to take power. At the same time, the much-beleaguered opposition had continued to lose countless state elections and their allegations of voting impropriety by the BJP fell mostly on deaf ears. Yet the emergence of the cockroaches has reinvigorated not only India’s youth, but its political opposition parties as well. Jumping on the bandwagon, the opposition Congress party has had its best week in years as it mobilised protests and shut down parliament. The party’s leader, Rahul Gandhi, was dramatically dragged away by police outside Modi’s house in support of students. Analysts say that dissent, which had been systematically crushed over the past 12 years, has now been re-galvanised as an effective tool to hold the government – and in particular the prime minister – to account. “After a long time, there’s an assertion of political agency across different sections of society,” said Mehta. “And the minute you see that agency out in the street, it empowers lots of other agents.” The next big test of the electoral implications of the CJP movement will come early next year, when India’s largest and most politically important state holds its state elections. Holding on to power in Uttar Pradesh, the BJP’s political heartland, is seen as crucial for the party and would have major implications for the next general election in 2029. The grievances of India’s newly-politicised youth are extensive, including a chronic lack of graduate jobs and stagnant wages. Just how the CJP intends to politically mobilise after its striking victory on Saturday remains to be seen. Leaders and supporters insist this is just the “beginning”, particularly in their push for education reform. Their founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has some past experience as a political party organiser, but has not made his own ambitions known. Yet analysts said that one of the most crucial impacts of the CJP had been to reopen a rapidly closing democratic space and make it seem possible that a new kind of political opposition could emerge, one reflective of the voices heard on the streets of India this week. Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said it was encouraging people involved in the movement to go into politics. “This is one of our goals,” he said. “We need to increase youth participation in politics, because right now it’s controlled by uncles and aunties who are only interested in looking after their own lifestyles and don’t understand the needs of our generation. The answer also has to be political.”

‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on power Prime minister’s propaganda machine falters as fiercely secular youth protests reclaim nationalism As the poster bearing the face of the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was thrown to the floor, a cheer went up. Then came the feet, trampling the image into the muddy ground with gleeful abandon. “Thief, thief,” chanted the crowd. Just a week earlier, such scenes in the heart of India’s capital would have been almost unthinkable. For the 12 years Modi and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) have been in power it was widely acknowledged that you criticised the government at your peril. Dissent was swiftly, routinely and expertly crushed. That was, until the cockroaches came along. A movement that began as an online meme has swiftly escalated into one of the most unexpected and significant challenges to Modi’s political power in years, instigated by a young generation who are fed up and startlingly unafraid of their government. Humour has become their greatest weapon and insults to Modi now abound online in the form of memes and Instagram reels as gen Z Indians vilify the government. Education, and the scandal over a leaked examination for medical colleges, remain at the heart of the protest, and the resignation of Modi’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, is the core demand. But after a peaceful protest held on Monday in Delhi was met with police batons, teargas, pellet guns and the alleged manhandling of female protesters, it has escalated into something far bigger: a fight for the country’s flailing democracy. Among those who braved the police response to take part in the Delhi demonstrations this week was Aniruddh Gautam, a 21-year-old law student from the capital. “I had a place to study at a UK university and I chose to stay in India because I believe in my country,” he said. “But this government has taken away the hopes and dreams of young people. Young people have died because of their failures. I will die for this cause if I need to.” While protests have erupted in India under the Modi government before – first in 2019 against a divisive citizenship law and then in 2020 with a huge farmers’ strike – analysts say the “cockroach” movement presents a more complex problem for the government. Education failures and exam leaks are uniquely bipartisan issues that concern even Modi’s most vital vote bank: upper-class Hindu families. The visuals of children and young students being beaten by police caused discomfort even among the BJP’s own ranks. “Modi has always been very good at overcoming a crisis,” said Tavleen Singh, a political columnist. “But I talk to people who are quite close to him and they’re all really puzzled and not sure what to do next. They say that he’s been listening to the wrong people and misread the mood completely.” While previous protests have been smeared by the government as the actions of Muslim or Pakistani terrorists, or sinister forces abroad, the fiercely secular nature of these demonstrations has made that impossible. Those taking part are from across religions and social classes and many of them are children of BJP supporters. At the Delhi protest site, Hindus and Muslims have prayed and eaten together. A Muslim cook has become a celebrity for feeding protesters every day and Sikh gurdwaras have set up community kitchens on site. “They are clever because they’ve made these protests deeply patriotic and taken back the nationalism card from the BJP,” said Singh. “They’ve also taken back secularism. These guys are using religion to unite.” Crucially, the BJP has come up against the limits of its own propaganda machine. While in the past decade mainstream media outlets have been co-opted to follow a strict government line, gen Z protesters have taken to social media to create their own information ecosystem, exposing the stark dissonance between what is being broadcast on mainstream news channels – referred to as godi, or lapdog, media – and what they are experiencing on the ground. “Our media is disgusting. Night after night they have broadcast lies to try and bring down our movement, calling us terrorists, Pakistanis and anti-nationals,” said Sanna, 26. “But unfortunately for them, we are here getting the message out.” Anish Gawande, a young politician who has been a champion of the cockroach movement, said the protests were erupting en masse because “increasingly, young people do not see a bright future for themselves in this country”. “An entire generation of aspirational young Indians grew up on the idea – and this includes me – that the country had flaws and needed to improve, but was on the whole heading towards progress,” he said. Now, he added, “we are confronted with the bitter reality that the whole story we were sold by the BJP in 2014 never materialised. The promises that have been made over the last 12 years have been repeatedly broken – and the crushing of that illusion is unleashing a pent-up rage unlike any other.” Gawande was insistent they posed an unassailable challenge to the BJP’s grip on power: “This is a rude awakening for the government that the people of India cannot be silenced forever.” When it first emerged in early May, it was easy for the government to dismiss the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), whose name was a deliberate poke at Modi’s ruling party. Its founder, Abhijit Dipke, 30, who had recently completed a masters at Boston University, initially created the CJP as a parody website in response to remarks by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches” during a court hearing (though he later denied saying it). The CJP’s original tagline was: “A voice for the lazy, unemployed and chronically online”. But when young Indians pounced upon it with delight, following in their tens of millions online, it became clear to Dipke that satire was proving more representative of their frustrations than mainstream politics. Two days before Kant’s alleged “cockroach” comment, the lives of more than 2 million students were upended when it emerged that a highly competitive exam for admission to medical college had been leaked and sold for millions of rupees. About 2.2 million students would have to take the gruelling test for a second time, competing for just 130,000 places. For some, it was too much to bear. More than a dozen took their own lives. It was not the first time this had happened: dozens of leaks had blighted these exams and others in recent years. The government had set up the private agency responsible, yet has never been held accountable. As he flew back into Delhi in early June, Dipke formalised the CJP’s core objectives: accountability for the exam leak, the resignation of Pradhan and the reform of a higher education system seen as chronically underfunded, corrupt and systematically failing millions of young Indians. The turnout at the CJP’s first Delhi protest was just a few hundred. But by the end of June, they returned, vowing they would not move from their Delhi protest site until Modi sacked his education minister. This time, the CJP had a new powerful figurehead. Sonam Wangchuk, a renowned Indian engineer and activist, announced that he would go on hunger strike in solidarity with the “cockroaches” – resonant of the hunger strikes made by Mahatma Gandhi in the fight for Indian independence. He too had come up against the Modi government’s crackdown on dissent, when he was jailed under terror laws for a protest last year. The Modi government initially met the protests with silence. But after the Delhi police aggressively removed Wangchuk on the 20th day of his hunger strike and dragged him to hospital against his will, popular outrage galvanised the movement. Delhi police, who are directly under the control of the home minister, Amit Shah, Modi’s closest political ally, had refused permission for protesters to march on parliament the following Monday. But that did not stop young people coming in unprecedented numbers. Delhi police prepared for 10,000 – an estimated 100,000 turned up, many chanting Wangchuk’s name. The demonstration was a critical turning point, an expression of dissent unlike anything seen in Delhi in years. For many of the young people, it was their first ever protest, marking something of a political awakening. They sobbed at the solidarity and fanned each other in the heat. But as the numbers swelled, the police were far outnumbered and began to resort to brutal tactics to prevent people marching on parliament. The use of teargas, batons and alleged pellet guns against young people made for horrifying footage, and hardened the position of many protesters. Among those targeted was 17-year-old Deeksha Mishra. She was there for her sister, whose dream was to be a doctor, but who had fallen into depression since the exam leaks. “I watched her losing her dream and passion and I knew I had to come,” she said. “We came peacefully but they treated us as terrorists,” she added. “The police beat us so badly. Some had blood flowing down their skulls and their noses were broken.” Hundreds ended up in hospital, some in intensive care. At the protest site days later, Mishra said she was now standing for more than just exam leaks. “This is about corruption, it’s about our dying democracy,” she said. “The government want to keep ignoring us until the protest dies but it’s not going to happen. We are not afraid any more.” While Modi has promised fast action against those responsible for the exam leaks, he has still refused to sack his minister. Analysts say he has been backed into a tricky corner: Pradhan is one of his most loyal and politically important ministers – to fire him could undermine cabinet loyalty and be seen as a sign of weakness for the strongman leader. Yet protesters say they won’t move until he’s gone. It remains to be seen just how much the movement has rattled the electoral grip of Modi, who still has three years left in office and recently won a string of crucial state elections. But as the political analyst and columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta said: “Most importantly, this movement has lifted the pall of fear.” “This government is used to governing with impunity,” he said. “Re-establishing unchallenged authority is going to be difficult for them.”

Here’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to come The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi The rebellion in India of the young, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), unfolded against a backdrop of large, abstract, geometrical structures – arcs, planes, hemispheres – that together make up an observatory called Jantar Mantar, built in the early 18th century to refine almanacs and tell time. Jantar Mantar has been a byword for political protest for decades: it marks the space that the Delhi police assigns to the politically disgruntled so they can vent in a contained way. But it had never before hosted a political insurgency that started from scratch and forced the Indian state to back down in less than eight weeks. When its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, brought the CJP to Jantar Mantar, it was a social media hashtag with 20 million followers. While he was studying in Boston, Dipke took the remarks of chief justice Surya Kant, who is accused of referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches”, and turned them into a here-we-come meme. When he brought the CJP home to Delhi on 6 June to make it real, people were intrigued. Given the mostly dismal fate of civil society movements during prime minister Narendra Modi’s time in office, no one anticipated the David and Goliath contest that came to a head last Saturday. Like other political tourists, I visited Jantar Mantar on 6 June out of curiosity. On that inaugural day it was modestly crowded and not that different from the dozens of demos I had attended over 50 years. The one difference was how young these so-called cockroaches were. I had seen young people mobilise against Modi’s government at close quarters before when the students of Jamia Millia Islamia, the university I taught in, came out against a pernicious citizenship bill. Their courage and idealism was defeated by a combination of police repression and organised rioting. This government’s willingness to use police brutality, vigilante violence and a pliant judiciary to snuff out protest hung over the fledgling CJP campaign like a shadow. But when I returned a month and a half later on 20 July, the scheduled day for the march to parliament, Jantar Mantar was unrecognisable. A hunger strike had raised the political temperature of the protest. The government had forcibly removed the main hunger striker, Sonam Wangchuk, from the site and detained him in a hospital. The calculation was that his absence would defuse the tension and demoralise the protesters. That didn’t happen. There were tens of thousands of people crammed into the barricaded space and thousands of police officers in attendance. The government had underestimated the size of the crowd that poured in by bus, train and car from Delhi and beyond. In the afternoon the Delhi police force and its masters compounded its miscalculation by attacking this giant gathering of young people with lathis (bamboo sticks) and teargas. This tableau of brutality was shocking enough in real life, but in the hands of young digital natives, whose phone cameras were extensions of themselves, it became a gush of online content that brought the violent drama of this confrontation into every home. The callous violence of the police and the raging, mocking, laughing defiance of the young protesters played out on every mobile phone. The cockroaches won where other protesters, not unlike them, such as Jamia’s students, had lost. They won, in part, because they weren’t visibly Muslim. There were Muslims among them, but this was a protest about the corruption of competitive examinations, an issue that concerns every middle-class family in India. It couldn’t easily be tarred as an anti-national conspiracy in the way that the struggle for secular citizenship led by Jamia’s mainly Muslim students was. This didn’t stop India’s mostly tame mainstream media from trying, but the scandal of the medical school examination was so egregious that no one gave them a hearing. Also, this was in the heart of New Delhi, a stone’s throw from parliament. Once the government had made, from its point of view, the cardinal error of letting gen Z occupy the commanding heights of the capital, every day of the protest produced hundreds of new episodes of a national drama – a digital Mahabharat – in which the vulnerable and charismatic children of light faced off against the armed and uniformed enforcers of darkness. Bharatiya Janata party governments have sanctioned massive police violence against minorities in India’s borderlands, in Manipur, Assam and Kashmir. But this was Jantar Mantar, the sacred centre of the republic. The leaders of the movement, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, had set themselves up for success by demanding a difficult but doable concession: the sacking of the education minister. It was difficult because Modi had never dismissed a cabinet minister in response to political pressure; this stubbornness was central to his strongman persona. It was doable because there were precedents in the history of the republic for a minister taking responsibility for a disaster and resigning. Modi did everything he could to wriggle out of this standoff. He even produced a comically inept Instagram video promising fast-track courts to address the corruption in the examination system. When that didn’t work, his government capitulated and Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister, departed. There was an assembly election scheduled in Uttar Pradesh next year and Modi knew that the BJP would haemorrhage political support if the Jantar Mantar impasse wasn’t resolved. The quarrel that some commentators on the left have with the CJP is that Pradhan’s dismissal was a symbolic victory but not a substantial one. Pralhad Joshi, the man who has replaced Pradhan as education minister, is not an improvement. Like Pradhan he is a member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the BJP’s far-right parent body. He publicly defended the premature release in 2022 of 11 men convicted for rape in the notorious Bilkis Bano gang-rape case. The CJP’s argument is that Pradhan was always a proxy for Modi. The point of the protest was to diminish Modi by forcing him to back down publicly. Also, it isn’t clear what a systemic victory would look like or how it would be achieved. The striking thing about the CJP’s leadership is its youth and poise. Zohran Mamdani, the youthful mayor of New York, now seems a template. He is 35. Dipke, the CJP’s Dalit leader, is 30 years old. Ashutosh Ranka, who negotiated the end of the protest with the BJP’s leadership, is about the same age. Das, the other negotiator and spokesperson, is all of 26. Neha Bora, the president of a leftwing student organisation, the All-India Students’ Association, is 25. It’s hard to know how their politics will evolve. What they have in common is eloquence, message discipline, all-round unflappability and the potential to leave a legacy. They may be an enduring problem for this government. Jantar Mantar may have just produced an echelon of homegrown Mamdanis.

The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics “What if all cockroaches come together?” was the question that humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It was posted on X by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. This weekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggested police officers attacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they have accused the government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally. Mr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism and demonising Muslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage. Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that has dominated the public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historian Mukul Kesavan says the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders. A similar kind of unrest during an anti-corruption movement in 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from the ruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot argues that the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Death and alleged torture of man in detention sparks protests in Syria Picture showing White Helmets volunteer unconscious and with bruises on his body went viral Syrians have protested over the death of a man who was arrested and allegedly beaten by security forces, sparking widespread anger at a practice thought to have ended with the fall of Bashar al-Assad. A crowd gathered in the city of Aleppo, demanding accountability for the security forces who are alleged to have carried out the torture, with participants holding signs and slogans such as: “Do not repeat the same oppression that we revolted against.” Protests were also planned to take place in front of Syria’s parliament in Damascus on Tuesday, as well. Mohammad Ghamira, a 29-year-old father of two and former volunteer in the White Helmets, had visited a police station in the coastal province of Latakia last week after an accusation of theft. Ghamira emerged from the station in a critical condition, and died in hospital on Sunday from “complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal haemorrhaging” that “resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained”, said Raed al-Saleh, the former head of the White Helmets and current Syrian minister of emergency and disaster management. A picture of Ghamira pre-detention, smiling and healthy, next to another picture of him unconscious in a hospital bed with bruises on his body, went viral, sparking outrage in Syria. Ghamira’s parents told the police station chief prior to their son’s detention that he had haemophilia, a disease which makes it hard to stop bleeding once started, and asked them not to beat him. Even with the warning, Ghamira was beaten while in custody, Issam Ghamira, the man’s uncle, told Syrian state media. The Syrian interior ministry promised accountability for Ghamira, forming a committee to investigate his death and detaining seven members of the interior ministry for questioning. The interior minister, Anas Khattab, vowed a “fair punishment” after the conclusion of the investigation. “I confirm that any violation or abuse by the elements of the ministry of interior will be dealt with firmly within the laws and procedures followed and any violator will receive his fair punishment,” Khattab said in a post on X. The interior minister spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba acknowledged issues in the ministry, but promised that justice would be served. Al-Baba said that the investigative committee met with family members on Tuesday and informed them of the progress of the investigation. Despite the promises of accountability, Syrians were incensed by the allegations of torture, enraged that the practice continued even after the 14-year revolution aimed at stopping such brutality. Al-Assad’s regime used mass detention and torture on a systematic scale to control its population, accelerating its brutality when protests broke out against the government in 2011. The current government, made up mostly of former members of the Islamist rebel group Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), overthrew al-Assad in a lightning offensive in December 2024. It promised an end to the atrocities committed under the police state that al-Assad oversaw, dismantling the dense network of security agencies that oversaw the country. However, rights groups have alleged that torture continues to be used in Syrian detention centres, and that the policy of abuse is being rebuilt. Syrians for Truth and Justice documented 14 cases of individuals being tortured or dying in custody from June 2025 to June 2026, and said that “the change in political authority has not yet been accompanied by the effective dismantling of the structures and practices that enable torture”. STJ collected testimonies that showed severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities by Syrian security forces across different agencies, often seemingly motivated by sectarian discrimination. The rights group pointed to a lack of oversight and accountability for militias and members of the security forces as an explanation for the persistence of torture in Syria, rather than a centralised policy of torture originating from security agencies themselves. It contrasted this with al-Assad’s regime, where torture was not due to gaps in law, but state policy itself. The report echoed the findings of the UN independent commission of inquiry in March, which documented torture and abuse in 30 official and makeshift detention facilities across Syria in 2025. Civil society groups called for protests and demanded accountability, pointing to the sacrifices of those who died under torture fighting for freedom in Syria. “So many sacrificed dearly for freedom and dignity, to close the dark chapter of their country’s history and to end these practices forever,” said Diab Serieh of the Association of Detainees and the Missing in Sednaya Prison. “Justice for [Ghamira], and for all those forcibly disappeared and under torture in detention, remains an unwavering demand that we will never abandon.”

‘Cockroach’ protests: India’s Modi promises to punish officials over exam leaks PM says ‘those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared’ as scandal spirals into widespread anger Narendra Modi has vowed to set up “fast-track courts” to speed up the punishment of officials accused of leaking examination papers, as the Indian prime minister seeks to quell a youth-led “cockroach” protest movement that has rocked Delhi and posed one of the biggest challenges to his government. In his first public remarks on the movement, Modi posted on X: “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth … Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared.” The offer of faster justice than usual from India’s clogged judicial system, which can take decades to deliver a verdict, was swiftly rejected by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), the satirical name the youth protest movement coined after India’s top judge called unemployed youths “cockroaches”. Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said: “It’s a Band-aid. That’s not giving us accountability. There have been zero convictions so far all these years, so this measure is of no use.” A core demand of the movement is the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, as well as reform of the education system. An estimated 50,000 people protested in Delhi on Monday, after police denied them permission to march on parliament. Officers later mounted baton charges and fired teargas. By Wednesday, more than 1,000 people remained camped at the CJP’s protest site in central Delhi despite the gruelling heat and humidity. Many had travelled long distances to be there. Renuka Chowdhury, an opposition MP with the Congress party, told the news channel India Today that no one could fathom why Modi would not sack Pradhan. “Honestly, is this one minister more valuable or more important than restoring harmony and order to the country?” he said. Modi’s statement follows signs the government may be softening its stance. Ministers have insisted they are willing to talk to the CJP but have refused to discuss Pradhan’s resignation. The protest site at Jantar Mantar has drawn crowds of supporters eager to show their solidarity. Unable to fit inside the enclosed area, many have spilled on to the surrounding roads. Some organise donations of food and water sent by wellwishers, while others distribute meals – including to the police on duty – fan those wilting from the heat or collect litter. Young people across India have also rallied behind the CJP’s demands, with three consecutive days of demonstrations in Mumbai and solidarity protests in Chennai, Indore, Hyderabad and Patiala. At a press conference on Wednesday, the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi escalated his criticism, demanding that in addition to Pradhan resigning, Modi should apologise for failing to provide a fair education system. Gandhi said there had been 152 exam paper leaks across the country over the past decade without a single conviction. “Somebody, or a group of people, are destroying our education system, India’s most valuable asset, destroying the lives of our students. What does the government do? Zero convictions,” he said. The health minister, JP Nadda, accused Gandhi of exploiting the protests for political gain. “Your concern is not to improve the education system, enhance the quality of education or ensure justice for students. Instead, you are trying to use students’ issues and their demands for political mileage. You are trying to derive political benefit from them, and that is unfortunate,” he said. CJP leaders were deeply disappointed after Monday’s meeting with Nadda – the first in over 60 days – ended without a breakthrough. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has since said that if ministers want to speak to them, they will have to come to the protest site and do so in public. Many in India are asking why Pradhan will not resign. Anish Gawande, an opposition politician, said Modi viewed backing down as a sign of weakness, particularly now that he no longer commands the parliamentary majority he enjoyed during his first two terms. “He is facing global headwinds that prevent him from executing any major reforms in agriculture, energy, the economy. The unemployment rate is climbing to levels not seen in three decades,” he said. “A show of weakness now will give an entry point for the opposition to move in and build a similar momentum around other issues […] Before you know it, things have spiralled out of control.”

Violence erupts in Belfast after protests over knife attack Crowds, including people in masks and hoods, burned vehicles and properties after calls for demonstrations from far-right figures Protests against immigration have erupted into violence in Northern Ireland after far-right activists called for demonstrations in response to a stabbing attack that was captured in a graphic video. Crowds including masked men burned vehicles and houses and blocked roads in and around Belfast on Tuesday night, hours after Elon Musk, Tommy Robinson and other agitators exhorted people to take to the streets. Protesters hijacked and burned a Glider bus on Newtownards Road in east Belfast and torched cars near Shankill Road and in Newtownabbey, from which smoke poured while sirens sounded and a police helicopter hovered above. The unrest flared hours after police charged a 30-year-old refugee from Sudan with attempted murder in connection with an attack in north Belfast on Monday night that left a man critically injured and prompted widespread shock and condemnation. The suspect is to appear at Belfast magistrates court on Wednesday. Ryan Henderson, the assistant chief constable, appealed for calm: “Sporadic pockets of disorder have broken out in a number of locations across Northern Ireland this evening, including incidents in which a number of vehicles have been set on fire. We are urging everyone to remain calm, act responsibly, and avoid any activity that could place themselves or others at risk.” Henderson asked for “all voices of influence” within local communities to encourage peaceful protest and to discourage violence or disorder. Politicians in Northern Ireland and across the UK also appealed for calm. Northern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, condemned the violence and warned of “dangerous attempts to exploit” the attack, saying in a social media post: “Groups of masked men burning families out of their homes is nothing less than disgusting cowardice. This has nothing to do with community. This is outright thuggery.” Earlier, O’Neill urged the public not to be persuaded by social media accounts to start causing disorder. “For all of those people out there who are stoking up tensions in that social media space, who are happy to raise tensions, they do not represent us. We are good people and I don’t want to see anybody living in fear.” John Finucane, the Sinn Féin MP for North Belfast, described the unfolding scenes as “shameful”, adding: “There is no place for it on our streets. Family homes and businesses attacked, cars and buses burned out, and parts of our community in flames. “No one has the right to spread fear, terrorise innocent families or bring lawless disorder on to our streets.” Northern Ireland’s Alliance justice minister, Naomi Long, said the demonstrators were “intent on wreaking destruction on the very communities they claim they are trying to protect”. Those interventions came as groups of men, some in balaclavas or other face coverings, launched fireworks and started fires in bins, buses and houses. In one flare-up near Shankill Road in Belfast, a group stormed a home that appeared to be occupied by a family from an ethnic minority background, claiming to be “liberating” it. Later, on the Shankill road, two phone shops had been looted, and an African shop had been set on fire, with smoke spilling into the street and fire engines stationed outside as a few stragglers braved the rain to watch the fire fighters tackle the flames. There were more muted protests in Antrim, Bangor, and Ballymena, and two cars were set alight in Newtownabbey. In London, a group of about 60 protesters gathered in Parliament Square, claiming that police were “traitors” and attempting to goad individual officers. Some shouted anti-immigrant slogans and chanted about the murder of Henry Nowak as well as the knife attack in Belfast. Most of the group protested peacefully. Politicians and community leaders accused the far right of seeking to foment unrest in Northern Ireland and across the UK. Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, a far-right agitator who refers to himself as Tommy Robinson, shared the video of the Belfast attack and posted a call for protests in central London and elsewhere in the UK. The stabbing happened at about 10.30pm on Monday outside a block of flats in north Belfast. Video shared on social media showed a man straddling another man on the ground and striking at his head and neck. A kitchen knife was recovered from the scene. Police said the victim, in his 40s, had serious injuries to his eyes, face and back. The clip showed people intervening to stop the assault, with one man, later named as Maitiu Mag Tighearnan, using a hurling stick against the attacker multiple times. In addition to attempted murder, the suspect was charged with possession of an article with a blade or point in a public place and threats to kill. I’ve been in direct contact with the head of terrorism policing in the UK. At this stage, we have no information to suggest that this was terrorist-related.” The chief constable asked protesters not to be goaded into disturbances: “People are incited by people who are faceless and know nothing about this brilliant, vibrant place. Do not be fooled or duped by people online.” Immigrant communities expressed fear that they would be targeted. Sudanese business owners on Sandy Row, a loyalist area of central Belfast, closed their stores with steel shutters by 4pm and said they planned to stay at home that night. The Belfast Islamic Centre cancelled evening prayers. “We are telling our congregation to go home, don’t go out, look after your children, don’t share rumours and do listen to the authorities,” said Ameer Ibrahim, a project manager who spoke in a personal capacity. Keir Starmer called Monday night’s attack sickening. “I have absolutely no tolerance for abhorrent scenes of violence like this on our streets. My thoughts are first and foremost with the victim, and I thank the first responders, including members of the public who intervened.” Rightwing commentators from England and the US, including the MP Rupert Lowe and billionaire owner of X Elon Musk, posted about the attack. Musk shared a list of potential protest areas in the UK and wrote: “Only by protesting REPEATEDLY and LOUDLY will there be any change!!” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said: “The horror of what you have seen in Belfast is a direct result of treacherous Tory and Labour immigration policy. More than 2m Indian students resit medical entrance exam after alleged leak Applicants forced to retake one of the world’s toughest admission tests after claims questions sold on Telegram More than 2 million aspiring Indian doctors have sat one of the world’s toughest entrance exams for a second time after an alleged question paper leak forced authorities to scrap the original test results. Students arriving at test centres on Sunday were greeted by airport-style security. They were frisked, scanned, checked biometrically and made to pass through metal detectors while police and paramilitary personnel stood guard outside. For many students, the retest turned an already gruelling ordeal into a nightmare. “One can only imagine the trauma each of you have gone through in the past few months,” news anchor Rajdeep Sardesai posted on X. One student said: “Thousands of students are emotionally exhausted after this long process. We are trying our best, but many of us are struggling mentally.” The test is the gateway to India’s medical colleges, where only about 5-6% of candidates secure a coveted seat. Many spend years preparing, attending expensive coaching classes and studying for long hours in the hope of making the cut. India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, promised a “fair and transparent” re-test, while the government has launched a sweeping investigation into the alleged questions leak last month. One candidate, Tarun, posted on X: “I did well but let’s see. The exam was tougher than last time.” The scandal led the government last week to temporarily suspend access to Telegram, one of India’s most popular messaging apps, after reports that leaked questions for the fresh exam were being sold on the platform. The ban drew criticism from internet free-speech advocates, but on Friday the company lost a court challenge when judges ruled the ban was justified. The medical test scandal is one of a long list of examination controversies that have shaken confidence in India’s vast testing machinery, which determines access to universities and government jobs for tens of millions of people each year and holds the promise of upward mobility for many. Earlier this month, more than 400,000 Indian students applied for copies of their test papers amid an outcry over marking errors in the country’s most important school-leaving exam after the introduction of a new digital scoring system. Teachers said when they were marking the exams, they were often still figuring out the software. The Indian Express newspaper asked why authorities “spend heavily on damage control instead of planning for prevention”, pointing to the costs of re-evaluations, reruns and the anxiety caused to students. A new Indian satirical group calling itself the Cockroach Janata Party (CPJ), a play on the ruling Bharatiya Janata party’s name, has stepped into the row. The CJP has become a lightning rod for frustration among students over exam glitches and lack of jobs for youth. “This failure cannot go ignored. There must be consequences,” said social media creator and CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. The movement has quickly amassed more than 22 million Instagram followers while, at demonstrations, protesters have demanded the education minister’s resignation.
